summary: Defines the ChaCha20 stream cipher and the Poly1305 authenticator, both separately and combined as an authenticated encryption (AEAD) algorithm. It introduces no new cryptography and serves as a stable reference for implementers. It was replaced by RFC 8439.

eli5.summary: A secret-scrambling recipe plus a tamper seal. The scrambler hides your message and the seal shows if anyone changed it along the way.

questions: when to use chacha20 instead of aes
subtitle: A modern stream cipher and authenticator for IETF protocols.

tldr.problem: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is the dominant cipher, but it has performance limitations on non-specialized hardware and is vulnerable to cache-timing attacks. A practical alternative cipher is needed for cases where AES is too slow or too risky.
tldr.mechanism: ChaCha20 is a stream cipher designed by D. J. Bernstein that is considerably faster than AES in software. Poly1305 is a one-time authenticator. Combined, they form an AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) algorithm suitable for protocols.
tldr.outcome: ChaCha20-Poly1305 is now widely deployed in TLS, IPsec, and other protocols as a modern, secure alternative to AES-based constructions. This reference was replaced by RFC 8439.

today: RFC 7539 is an Informational RFC that serves as a stable reference for implementations. It was replaced by RFC 8439. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is now widely deployed: it is a standard cipher suite in TLS 1.3, supported in IPsec, WireGuard VPN, and many other IETF protocols. It is the recommended alternative to AES-based constructions in environments where timing-attack resistance is important.

sections.title: Why a New Cipher for IETF Protocols
sections.content:
The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) has become the de facto encryption standard. It is fast on modern hardware with specialized support. However, AES has drawbacks. On platforms without AES hardware acceleration, it is considerably slower. More significantly, many AES implementations are vulnerable to cache-collision timing attacks, where variations in memory access patterns leak information about the encryption key.

ChaCha20, designed by D. J. Bernstein, offers a practical alternative. It is three times faster than AES on platforms without specialized hardware. ChaCha20 is also resistant to timing attacks because its operations—additions, XORs, and bit rotations—have constant execution time independent of the key.
sections.eli5: AES is very fast with special computer hardware, but slower without it. ChaCha20 is fast in both cases and does not leak secrets through timing variations.

sections.title: ChaCha20 Stream Cipher and Poly1305 Authenticator
sections.content:
ChaCha20 is a stream cipher that operates in 64-byte blocks. It takes a 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce, and a 32-bit block counter. The cipher generates a keystream by running 20 rounds of operations on a 512-bit state, alternating between column rounds and diagonal rounds. Each round applies four quarter-round operations. The output is XORed with the plaintext to produce the ciphertext. Decryption is identical: XOR the ciphertext with the same keystream.

Poly1305 is a one-time authenticator designed to produce a 128-bit tag (16 bytes) that authenticates a message. The key (32 bytes) is divided into two parts: r (clamped to specific bit positions for security) and s. The message is divided into 16-byte blocks, processed through modular arithmetic, and combined with s to produce the tag. Poly1305 provides strong unforgeability: an attacker cannot forge a valid tag even after seeing many legitimate messages.
sections.eli5: ChaCha20 generates a random-looking stream by mixing a key and counter 20 times. Poly1305 creates a small fingerprint that proves the message was not tampered with.

sections.title: Combined AEAD Algorithm
sections.content:
AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 combines ChaCha20 and Poly1305 into a single authenticated encryption algorithm. The process is:

First, a unique one-time Poly1305 key is derived from the 256-bit secret key and 96-bit nonce by running ChaCha20 with counter zero. Next, the message is encrypted using ChaCha20 with the same key and nonce, starting with counter one (counter zero is reserved for key generation). Finally, Poly1305 computes an authentication tag over a carefully constructed message that includes the additional authenticated data (AAD), the ciphertext, and length fields. The output is the ciphertext plus the 128-bit authentication tag.

A critical requirement: each invocation with the same key must use a unique nonce. If a nonce is repeated, both the keystream and the Poly1305 key are identical, and the XOR of the plaintexts is revealed.
sections.eli5: First, use ChaCha20 to generate a secret fingerprint key. Then encrypt the message. Finally, compute the fingerprint and send both the encrypted message and the fingerprint together.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
ChaCha20 is designed to provide 256-bit security. Poly1305 rejects forged messages with a failure probability of only 1/(2^102) per 16-byte message block. Both algorithms have undergone rigorous cryptographic analysis published in academic papers.

The most critical security requirement is nonce uniqueness. Nonces can be generated using a counter or Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR). A single nonce repetition catastrophically breaks security.

Implementation must be constant-time to avoid timing side-channels. ChaCha20 naturally fits this requirement because its operations (additions, XORs, rotations) are constant-time. Poly1305 requires care: modular arithmetic on 128-bit and larger numbers must not leak timing information about the key. Generic big-number libraries are unsafe; specialized constant-time implementations are essential.
sections.eli5: Never use the same nonce twice with the same key. Make sure your implementation does not leak timing information about the secret key.
